clue.text: Detective novel as modern oeuvre

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new or fresh, so the following letters take a new order

explanation.surface: A reviewer remarks that a detective story counts as a contemporary piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like the book the detective appears in, but it is the anagram signal for AS MODERN OEUVRE.
explanation.definitionFit: The full name of Colin Dexter's Oxford police inspector, known by his surname, whose first name was revealed late in the novels.

clue.text: Famous denial to Father Crilly

parts.note: a denial is a refusal, the word no
Father Ted Crilly is the priest in the sitcom Father Ted

explanation.surface: A celebrated refusal delivered to a hapless television priest.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Ted was a 1990s Channel 4 sitcom about an Irish priest, Ted Crilly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone noted is well known or celebrated, the same as being famous.

clue.text: Character introducing number of additives allowed by law in extract

parts.note: food additives are labelled with E numbers, so the letter E introduces each
licit means lawful, permitted

explanation.surface: Talk of an extract containing only the legal amount of food additives.
explanation.definitionFit: To elicit is to draw out or extract information or a response.

clue.text: Variety show provides remarkable value tempting one to come in

indicators.note: the tempter is asked to come in, entering the reshuffled word
remarkable read as re-markable: the letters are marked out again in another order

parts.note: the devil is the tempter of humankind

explanation.surface: A variety show offers wonderful value, luring the public inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remarkable' looks like praise for the value, but it signals the shuffle; 'to come in' tells the tempter to step inside the shuffled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaudeville is the American term for a stage entertainment of mixed acts, a variety show.

clue.text: Taxi service one needs right after underground fails to start

indicators.note: the letter for right comes after the shortened word
the underground's word loses its starting letter

parts.note: the Tube is London's underground railway

explanation.surface: A ride-hailing service is needed when the Tube breaks down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fails to start' takes T from TUBE, leaving UBE.
explanation.definitionFit: Uber is the app-based company whose drivers act as minicabs, a taxi service.

clue.text: Spots this person playing the part of Dawson

parts.note: the setter refers to themself, so this person is me
an actor appears as a character, playing the part
Les Dawson was a British comedian

explanation.surface: A setter notices themself cast as the comedian Dawson.
explanation.walkthrough: Les Dawson was a much-loved British TV comedian and game-show host.
explanation.definitionFit: The disease is known for its rash of red spots, so it can be called spots.

clue.text: Joey's acquiring digs showing spacious quality

indicators.note: the joey's word takes the digs into its middle

parts.note: a joey is a young kangaroo, a roo, so joey's gives roo's
mines are excavations, digs

explanation.surface: A young kangaroo finds lodgings with plenty of room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' looks like lodgings to suit the joey, but it means excavations; 'acquiring' takes them in before the possessive S.
explanation.definitionFit: Roominess is the property of having lots of space, a spacious quality.

clue.text: Brat tangling with lenient ref — his behaviour is embarrassing

indicators.note: the letters are tangled together and come out in a jumble

explanation.surface: A spoiled child argues with a soft referee and makes a scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tangling with' shuffles BRAT together with LENIENT REF.
explanation.definitionFit: French for terrible child, the phrase names a person whose unconventional conduct shocks or embarrasses others.

clue.text: What usherette must do because of love without response

definitions.meaning: a cinema usherette literally holds a flashlight to show patrons to seats
to love someone who does not return the feeling, an idiom

explanation.surface: A cinema attendant's duties, prompted by unrequited affection.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to harbour an unreturned passion; literally it is holding a torch for the audience.

clue.text: Trait — unusual trait shown by Scottish isle

indicators.note: unusual signals the letters set out in an uncommon order

parts.note: Bute is an island in the Firth of Clyde

explanation.surface: A distinctive quality observed in someone from a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges TRAIT into ATTRI.
explanation.definitionFit: An attribute is a characteristic quality, a synonym of a trait.

clue.text: A fruit dessert brought back with ice

indicators.note: the dessert's word is brought back, read from end to start

parts.note: a fool is a pudding of puréed fruit and cream

explanation.surface: A fruit pudding is returned, served with ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' turns FOOL into LOOF. 'with ice' describes a frosty manner.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who is distant and cold in manner can be said to behave icily.

clue.text: Man gets in case of rare Beaujolais perhaps

indicators.note: the man gets inside the outer letters
the case of a word is its outside letters

parts.note: Edwin is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man gets hold of a case of a rare vintage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case of' asks for the outside letters of 'rare', not a crate of wine; 'gets in' puts the man between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaujolais is an example of a French wine made from dark grapes.

clue.text: Football team, colourless, switching pair at the back

indicators.note: the last two letters of the word swap places

parts.note: an albino lacks pigment, so is colourless

explanation.surface: A dull football side reshuffles its central defenders.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the last two letters of ALBINO gives the name. West Bromwich Albion and Brighton & Hove Albion are English football clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Several English clubs carry the name, e.g. West Bromwich, so it can stand for a team.

clue.text: Copy exotic art prints around college

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go around the college letter
exotic suggests something strange, so the letters appear in a strange order

explanation.surface: Copies of foreign artworks are displayed around a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exotic' rearranges ART PRINTS into TRANSRIPT, which goes 'around' C.
explanation.definitionFit: A transcript is a written copy, especially of a record or of speech.

clue.text: A fuel for cookers

parts.note: gas is a fuel

explanation.surface: A type of fuel used in kitchen ranges.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a heavy British range cooker, a brand name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aga brand of range cooker is so well known that its name stands for such stoves.

clue.text: Farmer's second yield from croft — reap freely

indicators.note: freely means without constraint, so the letters move about

explanation.surface: A smallholder gets a second harvest by reaping a croft at will.
explanation.walkthrough: A croft is a small farm in Scotland. 'freely' rearranges CROFT and REAP.
explanation.definitionFit: An aftercrop is a second harvest taken from the same land in one season.

clue.text: Pests cried out abuse

indicators.note: out implies the letters are wrong or put out of place

explanation.surface: Annoying people shout insults.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cried out' looks like a phrase meaning shouted, but 'out' is the anagram signal for PESTS CRIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Disrespect, meaning rudeness or contempt, can amount to verbal abuse.

clue.text: Bachelor engaged in playing golf endlessly, working intermittently

parts.note: a show that is playing is on

indicators.note: the bachelor is engaged, taken inside the rest
the phrase for golf loses its final letter

parts.note: golf is played on the links

explanation.surface: An unmarried man busy at golf, but his play keeps faltering.
explanation.walkthrough: Golf is played on 'the links', a seaside course; 'endlessly' drops its last letter and 'engaged in' slips the bachelor in before the final word.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a device that is faulty and only works on and off.

clue.text: Learned English getting offensive about it

indicators.note: the offensive word goes about, around, the other piece

parts.note: rude means offensive

explanation.surface: An English person turns nasty over something.
explanation.definitionFit: Learned, said as two syllables, means scholarly and well-read, as is an erudite person.

clue.text: Emperor Haile Selassie's follower mostly rejected

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, read backwards
most of the word, losing its last letter

parts.note: Rastafarians revere the Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie

explanation.surface: An emperor's devotee is largely spurned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' leaves RAST from RASTA; 'rejected' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsar was the emperor of Russia.

clue.text: Test bid for business round railway

indicators.note: the bidding word goes round the railway letters

parts.note: to tout is to solicit custom

explanation.surface: An attempt to win custom for a firm on the railways.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryout is a trial or audition, a test of ability.

clue.text: Former sprinter tailed after body found in Cambridge college

indicators.note: the trimmed sprinter comes after the body

parts.note: corpus is Latin for body and an English word for a body of work

indicators.note: tailed means with its tail cut off, losing the last letter

parts.note: Linford Christie was a British Olympic 100 metres champion

explanation.surface: A former athlete's corpse is found in a Cambridge college.
explanation.walkthrough: Linford Christie won 100m gold for Britain in 1992; 'tailed' drops his final E.
explanation.definitionFit: This college, named for the feast of the Body of Christ, is one of the colleges of Cambridge University.

clue.text: See 22
Surreptitious activity reported in Irish county town

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the phrase is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: sly means sneaky and a go is a turn of activity

explanation.surface: Secret goings-on reported in an Irish provincial town.
explanation.definitionFit: This town in north-west Ireland is the administrative seat of the county of the same name.

clue.text: Wilder element that's inherited

definitions.meaning: ... Wilder was an American actor, star of Willy Wonka
a unit of heredity passed from parent to child

explanation.surface: A more untamed component passed down the generations.
explanation.definitionFit: The actor Wilder's first name is also the biological unit of heredity.

clue.text: Asian language, remote, is from the East

parts.note: far means distant, remote

indicators.note: in an across entry, coming from the east means reading right to left

explanation.surface: A distant Asian tongue arriving from the Orient.
explanation.definitionFit: Farsi is the Persian language of Iran.

clue.text: Article backing trend I set in test

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a tide of opinion is a trend

indicators.note: the I is set inside the test word

parts.note: an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece supporting a fashion I established in an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns TIDE into EDIT; 'set in' puts I into ORAL to make ORIAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A leading article in a newspaper giving the paper's opinion is called an editorial.

clue.text: Treat pensioner for moving picture

indicators.note: moving the letters around puts them in a new order

explanation.surface: Give an elderly person a trip to see a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving picture' reads as a film, but 'moving' is the anagram signal and 'picture' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A representation is a depiction or image, such as a picture or portrait.
